title: Algorithmic Problem Solving: Longest Common Prefix String Scanning
concepts_and_definitions: Longest Common Prefix (LCP) – the longest string that is a prefix of all input strings
Binary Search – a divide‑and‑conquer technique used to find the maximum prefix length efficiently
Hash Set – a data structure used to count character occurrences across strings for LCP detection
Time Complexity – analysis of algorithmic performance, e.g., O(n*m) for naive LCP, O(n*log m) for binary search
Garbage Collection in Java – automatic memory management and reference counting concepts discussed in context of string handling
mechanisms_and_formulas: Binary Search on prefix length: low=1, high=minLen, mid=(low+high)/2, check if prefix of length mid is common
Hash Set frequency counting: for each character position, map char->count, common if count==numStrings
Time complexity of naive LCP: O(n*m) where n is number of strings and m is average string length
examples_and_code_patterns: Iterative character comparison loop that builds a StringBuilder and breaks on mismatch
HashSet based LCP implementation in Java that clears the map after each character position
Binary search based LCP implementation in Java that adjusts low/high based on prefix existence
factual_summary_text: The lecture revisits two classic algorithmic problems: the Longest Common Prefix (LCP) and the Cocoa Eating Bananas problem. For LCP, the instructor contrasts a naive character‑by‑character scan with more efficient approaches. A hash‑set solution is shown, where a map counts occurrences of each character at a given position across all strings; if the count equals the number of strings, the character is part of the common prefix. The lecture also covers a binary‑search strategy that treats the prefix length as a search space, repeatedly testing whether a candidate length is common and narrowing the bounds until the maximum length is found. Throughout, code snippets in Java illustrate the logic, including loop structure, map clearing, and string building. Memory management in Java is briefly discussed, emphasizing that objects become eligible for garbage collection when no references remain, unlike explicit deallocation in C/C++. The Cocoa Eating Bananas problem is introduced as a binary‑search application: given piles of bananas and a time limit, the goal is to find the minimal eating speed that allows all bananas to be consumed within the allotted hours. The instructor walks through a brute‑force approach and then hints at a binary‑search solution, reinforcing the theme of efficient search over a monotonic property. The session ends with a review of code improvements, such as avoiding unnecessary object creation and clarifying loop exit conditions, to produce clean, maintainable Java code.
